Forced: neither idea works; coffee shouldn't read as sea or water, and both look like fabric softener or soap packaging. The brand name pushed the sea theme.

Grabs attention and gets the idea across at a glance.

Easier to take in, but its official header has no character: official pieces need the real logo or they look like a children's project. Black text gets lost on the red; white would be better. The other is too busy.
A toss-up; this one is composed better.
More original idea, but the climber is lost in the scene: dark clothes on a wall of the same tone don't read from a distance. The other's lone shoe at the wall could read as an accident.
Its central title reads better; the spirit and gist win despite its problems. The other's illustration is tighter, but its title fights the moon and the layout is unbalanced.
Both meet the brief and fall short equally; they read as the same character, one slightly older but still young.
Both look equally amateurish; this one gets the information across more strongly, and the name at the top reads as an official say-so for an on-site notice, not as advertising. Bland.
Clearer information, though not nice to look at; the issuer's real branding would have been better.

Very close; both are very good, balanced and official. This one wins on looks (a big phone screen, icon flair) but invents app screens; the other follows the brief exactly, is more thoughtfully tuned and would win if the brief means finished work.

Close and reluctant. This one's type is better balanced, easier on the eye and warmer, but it reads as pulpy young-adult fiction; the other is clean, cold and distant and reads as a true classic, and its mood of light in a glasshouse may suit the book.
Reads instantly at thumbnail size; better balance, great flow, and it shows the event. The instruction to wear something bright should also be in the text, not only implied by the art.

Clear winner: more dynamic and tight; the stormy, slightly yellowed light fits, the two small figures huddled together are warm, and the quiet speech against the loud rain is evocative. But the speech text is too small and blends into the soil at a distance, and there is no hint of school. The other has an amateurish glow round its text and forces the school into the scene.
The other is less dense and readable and turns the steps into easy panels, but a catastrophic failure in its third panel forces a fail.

Cute, readable and personable; more eye-catching and informative at a glance. Aside: a full-colour 3D render is likely costly or wasteful for a council to print, and 'One day later' in the box's empty space feels slightly unbalanced.
No reason given.

This one, though the art is too clean, refined and clinical for a children's book; children's media tends to be livelier. The author name at the bottom left is mildly bothersome: it would be better centred and in white.

Evokes a traditional jam and gets the gist across at once, though writing 'small family farm' on the label literally is silly. The other is too contemporary and out of place, with an unattractive stroke round the dark fruit on its dark ground.
Shows the trait through gesture and is more charming; the other is overdone and hyper-literal.
Wins on many counts: tighter, cleaner art, a cohesive story, and the picture follows the action. The other over-applies the words and shows two planes where the brief's 'it' means one.
Very clean, concise yet dynamic art; the other has a glowing, over-detailed chocolate-box painting style that is too busy for the eye.
The winner, though its title is too loud and punchy: the scene calls for a measured coldness. The other is too compact and hyper-literal, if traditionally evocative.
Better by miles.
Sells the concept in gesture alone, with a tight, dynamic, expressive pose; the other tries to explain it in text.
Close; this one, slightly.
Balanced, easy to read at a distance and high in contrast: very well designed and effective for its job, though not flawless. Menus reward design that is easy to take in.
A moderate pick: the other is very busy, but this one is perhaps a bit too sparse.

Forced. This one is basic text only, and its yellow call to action on a bright ground is ugly and dense. The other is better, but its solid block in the centre and lopsided graphic at the bottom look amateur, even like a printer's misalignment.
Academically tight but bland and sterile; the other is very busy but has a fantastical, cosy quality. Picked this one anyway.
Cleaner to the eye: information economy, stable characters, clear warnings, fit for purpose.

Punchier type and an unbroken, cohesive trail; more fun. Neither is true to the loop and the bridge (start = finish should read as a loop, and a river crossing should show a bridge). The other has a nice centred, official park-leaflet look.
Better balance, an appropriate amount of information, more pleasing. The other suits short, practical water-safety notes but is not pleasing to the eye.
Both decent; this one fits the age range better. The title is not lost, but not as punchy as it could be.
Dynamic and eye-catching. The other is accurate but sterile, like a PowerPoint slide.
Tough call. Its specific diagrams are more useful to a reader who came for the information. The other is easier to read but repeats the same image in every panel: repetitive and wasteful.
On vibes: stylish, a nice layout, a good amount of visual busyness, though it overuses the bakery's name and the illustrations look sloppy. The other is too basic.
A judgement call, for its emotional direction: it reads like real nutrition information on a bar's packaging, personal. The other is matter-of-fact and sterile, though a fact sheet may want that.
Both good; this one is cleaner, with punchier illustrations.
Clean and direct. The other's art direction is busy and visually chaotic.
